vignette:
Javier is a man who built his life on predictability. For thirty years as a tax consultant, he found comfort in the neat columns of a spreadsheet, the clear logic of the fiscal year. Now, at fifty-three, his world is governed by a different, more chaotic calculus of risk. The logic that once defined him has been replaced by a persistent, humming dread that dictates his every move. His divorce was finalized a year ago, a quiet casualty of the man he became after the protest.

It happened two years ago. Javier had never been an activist, but a proposed zoning change threatened his neighborhood, and he joined the march to city hall, a cardboard sign in his hands. The mood was peaceful until the police line advanced. He remembers the shift in the air, the sudden press of bodies. He saw a young woman stumble and fall, her forehead split open and bleeding onto the grey pavement. As he moved to help her, a surge of officers pushed through the crowd. An arm swung, a baton connected with his shoulder, and the world became a universe of white-hot pain and the grinding sound of his own bones. He remembers lying on the ground, pinned by the weight of his own helplessness, watching the chaos unfold as if through a tunnel.

That searing pain in his shoulder is a constant, unwelcome companion. Sometimes it’s a dull ache, other times a sharp twinge, but either way, the sensation pulls him instantly back to the pavement. A flare-up of this old injury is enough to trigger a cascade of self-recrimination; he had come to believe there was something intrinsically weak about him, some fault in his character that had invited the violence. Seeing someone else with a visible injury—a man with a bandaged hand on the subway, a child with a scraped knee at the park—has the same effect, plunging him into a state of shame and confirming his belief that he is fundamentally different, set apart from those who navigate the world unscathed.

This deep-seated conviction that he is uniquely broken and vulnerable has transformed the world into a landscape of imminent threat. Because he believes he is incapable of protecting himself, he cannot enter a new building without first identifying every possible exit. He has turned down several new, lucrative clients simply because their offices were in unfamiliar parts of the city, a risk his mind will not allow him to take. When he walks the few blocks from his apartment to his office, he finds himself constantly checking behind him, certain that he is being followed. He sees danger not as a possibility, but as an inevitability he is unequipped to handle, a direct consequence of his perceived personal failing.

This constant state of high alert is exhausting, and it only serves to reinforce his most painful beliefs. Every time he has to consciously map the path to the door in a quiet library, it serves as another piece of evidence that he is no longer a normal person, deepening the chasm of isolation that separates him from everyone else. This relentless vigilance leaves him so drained that the thought his life may not be worth living has begun to feel less like a dramatic fear and more like a logical conclusion. His hyper-awareness also makes the world a minefield; by constantly scanning for threats, his attention is invariably snagged by the very things that wound him most—a news report about police brutality, a stranger’s bruised face—ensuring he is never far from a reminder of his own trauma.

Javier sought therapy after his daughter, visiting from out of state, gently pointed out that he hadn't been to a restaurant or store outside of a four-block radius in over a year. The observation landed with the weight of a final judgment. He confessed that his carefully constructed world had become a prison, and he was now more afraid of his own mind than of any external threat. His greatest fear, he admitted in a quiet voice, is that the man who understood numbers and logic is gone forever, leaving only this terrified stranger in his place.
